method: Compared excerpts against claim-bearing local scripture passages, independently from drafting. Not a historical or theological adjudication.

revisions.title: The Family of Noah
revisions.finding: Calling the drunkenness and curse merely an 'incident' followed by 'words' removes the substance of this half of the passage. Naming Ham's seeing Noah and the curse on Canaan is clearer without adding an explanation for the curse.

revisions.title: Hagar and Ishmael
revisions.finding: The wording 'conflict with Sarai sends' obscures the immediate cause: Sarai deals harshly with Hagar, who flees. The angel also commands her return, rather than merely promising descendants. This is a precision improvement, not a claim that the original contradicts every detail.

revisions.title: Jacob and Esau
revisions.finding: Finding a wife is a stated reason for the journey, but Esau's specific death threat and Rebekah's instruction to flee are also central. Merely mentioning anger before a marriage trip understates the danger driving Jacob's departure.

revisions.title: Jacob Returns to Canaan
revisions.finding: The final sentence removes only 'then' from the existing summary sentence. Its facts are sound, but it is an almost verbatim copy rather than independently phrased preview text.

revisions.title: Judah and Tamar
revisions.finding: 'Father of her pregnancy' is unnatural English. Also specify that two sons die, since Shelah remains alive and his withheld marriage is the point of Tamar's complaint.

revisions.title: Joseph in Egypt
revisions.finding: The opening makes dream interpretation seem responsible for Joseph's recognition throughout Potiphar's household and prison. Genesis 39 attributes his advancement there to successful service; dream interpretation starts with the prisoners in chapter 40 and reaches Pharaoh in chapter 41.

revisions.title: The Birth and Rescue of Moses
revisions.finding: The basket does not carry Moses toward the princess. His mother places it among reeds at the bank; Pharaoh's daughter notices it and sends her servant to fetch it.

revisions.title: Nadab and Abihu
revisions.finding: Moses forbids particular mourning gestures, not all grief or mourning as a mental state. The verse explicitly permits the wider community to mourn. Naming the gestures preserves that distinction.

revisions.title: The Twelve Spies
revisions.finding: The sentence about 'that generation' facing death fails to identify the two named exceptions and can include the children, who are expressly promised entry. Specify the older generation and Joshua and Caleb's exemption.

revisions.title: Vengeance on Midian
revisions.finding: The excerpt stops at Moses objecting that women survived, then jumps to goods and an offering. It omits his command to kill captured boys and women who have slept with men, retain the virgin girls, and divide human captives. These are material parts of the passage, not incidental details.

revisions.title: Tribes Settle East of the Jordan
revisions.finding: Only Reuben and Gad present the request in verses 1-5 and negotiate the condition. Half of Manasseh receives land in the later allocation; the text does not include it in the initial petition.

revisions.title: Joshua Commissioned and the Law Entrusted
revisions.finding: The song's stated purpose is to serve as a witness against Israel when the people abandon the covenant, not simply to remind them of a duty. The original also omits the elders from the recipients of the law, though that omission alone is not material.

revisions.title: The Fall of Jericho
revisions.finding: Joshua declares the destruction before the walls fall (verse 17 before verse 20), not afterward. The chapter then describes killings and burning, not merely a decision to set the city apart. The replacement preserves the promised rescue of Rahab's household without softening the city's fate.

revisions.title: Achan's Sin and Ai
revisions.finding: Achan takes a robe, silver and gold. Jericho's precious metals were reserved for the treasury (Joshua 6:19), not destruction. 'Forbidden goods' covers the common prohibition without assigning the wrong destination to the metals.

revisions.title: Gideon and the Midianites
revisions.finding: Ending the account on refusal of kingship leaves out its immediate reversal: Gideon makes a gold ephod, which Israel worships and which becomes a snare to his household. Because the preview chooses the concluding leadership episode, retaining this counterpoint better represents the actual ending. The new wording also limits the 300 men's victory to the initial rout, before other Israelite troops join the pursuit.

revisions.title: Jephthah's Vow
revisions.finding: The central outcome of the titular vow is missing. Judges 11:39 says that Jephthah does to his daughter according to his vow. Report that wording rather than silently dropping the outcome or adding a disputed explanation of precisely how it was fulfilled.

revisions.title: The Levite and Gibeah
revisions.finding: 'Arrange wives' conceals the means: killing the people of Jabesh-gilead except virgin girls and giving those captives to Benjamin, followed by abductions of women at Shiloh. The apparent neutral wording changes the moral substance of the ending.

revisions.title: Ruth Gleans in Boaz's Field
revisions.finding: The current final sentence suggests a distinct gift of grain in addition to gleaning, resembling the six measures in Ruth 3:15-17. In chapter 2 Boaz directs workers to leave extra grain for her to glean and provides a meal. Specify the actual means of help within this passage.

revisions.title: The Threshing Floor
revisions.finding: The first sentence closely reproduces the existing summary, chiefly changing 'On' to 'Following' and 'at' to 'on'. Its facts are supported; the replacement supplies independent phrasing without asserting a sexual encounter or an immediate unconditional marriage promise.

revisions.title: Samuel Judges Israel
revisions.finding: The new opening locates the instruction to abandon foreign gods at Mizpah. The instruction and the people’s response occur in verses 3–4, before Samuel calls the gathering at Mizpah in verse 5.

revisions.title: Saul Rejected
revisions.finding: “An early sacrifice” can imply that Saul did not wait the specified seven days. Verse 8 says he waited seven days; the concrete fact is that he sacrificed before Samuel arrived.

revisions.title: David, Bathsheba and Uriah
revisions.finding: “Bathsheba’s first child” asserts her complete birth history. The passage identifies the child born to David, but does not say Bathsheba had never had another child.

revisions.title: Sheba's Revolt and the Gibeonites
revisions.finding: “Treatment” and “handed over” omit the killings central to the famine episode. Saul had killed Gibeonites; David hands over seven descendants, and the Gibeonites execute them. The first sentence can also preserve the townspeople’s role in ending Sheba’s revolt.

revisions.title: Elisha and Moab
revisions.finding: The ending omits the allied withdrawal immediately following the sacrifice. With a prediction of victory as the preceding sentence, omitting the retreat hides the account’s crucial reversal. Do not identify the cause or owner of the “wrath,” which the verse leaves unspecified.

revisions.title: Naaman Healed
revisions.finding: Gehazi does not simply accept a reward. Elisha refuses a gift; Gehazi lies to obtain one and then lies to Elisha about it. Omitting the deception changes the apparent reason for his punishment.

revisions.title: Jehu's Revolt
revisions.finding: “Brings down” obscures that Jezebel, Ahab’s family and Baal’s worshipers are killed, not simply removed from power. Distinguishing Jehu’s direct killing of Joram from his orders concerning Ahaziah also improves precision.

revisions.title: Solomon Builds the Temple
revisions.finding: Fire does not fill the temple. The passage distinguishes fire consuming the offerings from the LORD’s glory filling the house. The underlying summary has the same conflation.

revisions.title: Sennacherib's Invasion and Hezekiah's Pride
revisions.finding: “Is brought low” replaces Hezekiah’s voluntary humbling with an unspecified external defeat. Verse 26 says that he and Jerusalem’s inhabitants humble themselves and that wrath does not come during his lifetime.

revisions.title: Ezra and Mixed Marriages
revisions.finding: The agreement covers the wives and their children, not wives alone. Omitting the children understates the scope and consequence of the separation described in Ezra 10:3.

revisions.title: Nehemiah's Reforms
revisions.finding: “The Sabbath gates” invents a type or name of gate. These are Jerusalem’s city gates, closed before and throughout the Sabbath.

revisions.title: Haman's Plot
revisions.finding: “A decree against all Jews” and “seek” weaken a decree that is actually issued to kill them. Naming the threatened killing is essential to understanding Esther’s action and risk.

revisions.title: The Jews Delivered and Purim
revisions.finding: Mordecai receives the king’s signet and authority in Esther 8:2–10, before the defensive decree and fighting, not only after the threat passes. Also, “those attacking them” is narrower than the narrative’s enemies or people seeking their harm.

revisions.title: Jerusalem and the Ark
revisions.finding: The excerpt mentions Uzzah’s death without the ark-touching action or God’s agency, turning the central incident into an unexplained interruption. This is not a factual contradiction, but the cause is more useful than “transfer interrupted.”

revisions.title: The Davidic Covenant
revisions.finding: “House” shifts from building to dynasty without explaining that change. “Royal line” preserves the passage’s meaning for readers without biblical background.

revisions.title: Solomon Becomes King
revisions.finding: “Removes his rivals” hides the executions and the priest’s dismissal. A short, direct alternative can describe the outcome without listing every death.

revisions.title: The Man of God from Judah
revisions.finding: “Disobeys” omits the other prophet’s explicit lie, and “dies in an encounter” is less clear than the source’s “a lion ... killed him.” Including the deception avoids implying unexplained willful rebellion.

revisions.title: Elijah on Mount Carmel
revisions.finding: The passive account of the prophets’ deaths omits Elijah’s explicit responsibility. This is not an invented claim, but active wording better preserves the account’s difficult events.

revisions.title: Elijah Taken Up
revisions.finding: “Fire falls on soldiers” omits both Elijah’s call and the soldiers’ deaths. The rest of the excerpt is sound, including the whirlwind rather than an invented ride in the fiery chariot.

revisions.title: Manasseh's Repentance and Josiah's Reforms
revisions.finding: “Dies in battle” blurs the version in Chronicles: Josiah is wounded in battle, carried to Jerusalem, and dies there. The distinction matters because Kings instead reports him carried dead from Megiddo.

revisions.title: Debt Relief
revisions.finding: Debt “costs ... their children” can suggest deaths. The specific harm is debt slavery, stated explicitly in Nehemiah 5:5.

revisions.title: The Fall of Jerusalem and Flight to Egypt
revisions.finding: The first sentence introduces Jeremiah’s warning before the second introduces Gedaliah’s death. The literal clauses are not incompatible, but they invite a mistaken sequence. Gedaliah is killed before the survivors seek Jeremiah’s counsel.

revisions.title: The Death of Ezekiel's Wife
revisions.finding: Saying the LORD merely warns Ezekiel softens the stated divine agency: 'I will take away from you the desire of your eyes.' 'About the sanctuary and their families' also hides the threatened defilement and deaths. This is an omission/clarity concern, not a contradictory stated fact.

revisions.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
revisions.finding: Daniel 6 describes officials plotting after Daniel is favored for promotion, but does not state jealousy. Presenting them as jealous converts an inferred motive into fact.

revisions.title: Hosea's Marriage to Gomer
revisions.finding: The excerpt says the marriage is commanded and the names are symbolic, without saying what either signifies. The passage explicitly compares Israel's religious unfaithfulness with adultery and contrasts judgment on Israel with mercy for Judah. Suggested for clarity, not as a factual correction.

revisions.title: Jonah Flees and Is Swallowed
revisions.finding: The sailors throw Jonah overboard at his own request and only after unsuccessfully trying to row ashore. Adding 'at his request' preserves their role and avoids an impression of an unprompted attack.

revisions.title: Sabbath Controversies and the Sign of Jonah
revisions.finding: The question about healing on the Sabbath precedes the healing in Matthew 12:10-13. Saying questions follow both the grain picking and healing reverses that second sequence.

revisions.title: Feeding the Five Thousand and Walking on Water
revisions.finding: Matthew counts about five thousand men in addition to women and children, not an exact total of five thousand. Preserve that scope when using the count in prose.

revisions.title: The Paralytic and Controversies
revisions.finding: Mark identifies four people carrying the man but never says they are his friends. That familiar retelling detail should not be asserted as part of this passage.

revisions.title: Feeding the Multitude
revisions.finding: Mark 6:44 counts five thousand men. 'A crowd of five thousand people' turns that into a total headcount. Do not import women and children from Matthew into this Mark-specific excerpt; retain Mark's own wording.

revisions.title: Blind Bartimaeus
revisions.finding: The second sentence repeats that Bartimaeus called out rather than adding the text's resolution: he follows Jesus. This is a prose improvement, not a factual correction.

revisions.title: The Empty Tomb
revisions.finding: A stone 'meets' the women is awkward personification. The excerpt also omits the distinctive ending of the specified Mark 16:1-8 range: the women say nothing to anyone despite the instruction to tell the disciples. Suggested for clarity and completeness.

revisions.title: Noahic Covenant
revisions.finding: The excerpt names the rainbow and recipients but never states the covenant's promise: no flood will again destroy all life. Suggested for useful standalone card content, not because its stated facts are false.

revisions.title: Priestly Covenant with Phinehas
revisions.finding: 'Phinehas's action' and 'the event' hide the killing of an Israelite man and Midianite woman that precedes this promise. That omission particularly obscures the relationship between violence and the 'covenant of peace.' The killing is in immediately preceding Numbers 25:7-8, outside the current linked range; expand its contextual citation if this detail is included.

revisions.title: Davidic Covenant
revisions.finding: Calling Psalm 89 a 'later psalm' adds a compositional chronology that the cited passages do not establish. It is enough to identify the psalm and what it recalls. This is a qualification concern, not a claim that the proposed dating is necessarily false.

revisions.title: New Covenant
revisions.finding: The coordinated subject 'Luke and Hebrews' makes both sources seem to quote/revisit Jeremiah and contrast old and new covenants in the same way. Luke 22:20 connects the cup with the new covenant; Hebrews explicitly quotes Jeremiah and contrasts the covenants. Preserve those distinct contributions and Jeremiah's named recipients.

revisions.title: Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet
revisions.finding: The opening is effectively the existing summary sentence with 'During' changed to 'At' and punctuation changed. Normalized character similarity is about 95%; no complete sentence in the reviewed range is an exact normalized copy.

revisions.title: Rejection at Nazareth
revisions.finding: The jump from the Isaiah claim to violence omits the intervening examples of outsiders helped by Elijah and Elisha. Luke links the anger to those examples, not directly to the reading.

revisions.title: The Sinful Woman Anoints Jesus
revisions.finding: The woman washes with tears, wipes with her hair, and anoints with ointment. Washing with tears and oil merges separate actions.

revisions.title: Zacchaeus
revisions.finding: The excerpt treats cheating as an established confession. Zacchaeus states a conditional promise: if he has taken anything by false accusation, he restores it fourfold. Preserve that qualification.

revisions.title: The Woman Caught in Adultery
revisions.finding: The central outcome is missing: the accusers leave, Jesus declines to condemn her, and he tells her to stop sinning. Sends the woman away loses this resolution.

revisions.title: Breakfast by the Sea of Tiberias
revisions.finding: John explicitly depicts Jesus giving bread and fish to the disciples. It does not explicitly say he eats with them. Serving breakfast avoids adding an action.

revisions.title: The Lame Man Healed and Arrest of Peter and John
revisions.finding: While suggests the believers pray during the council hearing, but Acts places the prayer after release. Peter also expressly denies healing by their own power; name Jesus in the healing.

revisions.title: Saul's Conversion
revisions.finding: The conversion is reduced to light and a restored disability. The voice identifying itself as Jesus supplies the narrative link between Saul persecuting believers and preaching Jesus.

revisions.title: The Jerusalem Council
revisions.finding: Whether ... brings is awkward. More importantly, only a few requirements does not answer the question the excerpt raises: the letter rejects the imposed circumcision requirement.

revisions.title: Ephesus
revisions.finding: Two years specifically describes teaching in the school after three months in the synagogue; Paul later recalls three years. Avoid making two years the apparent total teaching period.

additional_resolution: Cain excerpt avoids assigning a motive to potential killers; Phinehas passage expanded to Numbers 25:7–13.
